questions.stem: How do document databases store data?
options: As JSON-like documents that can contain nested fields, arrays and variable structures
As rows and columns in normalised tables
As nodes and edges
As owner–member sets with pointers
As columns grouped into families and partitioned by key
questions.explanation: Document databases treat each document as a self-contained representation of a business object, with nested fields, arrays and variable structure.

questions.stem: What does a single document typically represent in a document database?
options: One column of a table
One business object, such as an entire loan application
One transaction log entry
One index entry
One relationship between two entities
questions.explanation: Each document typically represents one business object; in a loan approval system a single document may represent an entire loan application with embedded customer, officer and repayment data.

questions.stem: In the MongoDB loan example, how is the repayment history represented inside the loan document?
options: As a foreign key to a Repayment collection
As a comma-separated string field
As an array of Repayments, each with its date and amount
As a nested LoanOfficer object
As a separate top-level document per instalment
questions.explanation: The loan document contains an array of Repayments that stores each instalment with its date and amount alongside the nested Customer and LoanOfficer objects.

questions.stem: Why do document databases align naturally with API payloads?
options: Because they enforce strict schemas
Because they require joins before serving data
Because they store data in relational tables
Because the data is already in JSON format
Because they use SQL for queries
questions.explanation: Since documents are stored as JSON, the structure aligns naturally with API payloads and mobile or web applications can display data without multiple joins.

questions.stem: Why can adding a new field to a document database be done easily?
options: Because every field is stored as a separate table
Because new fields are ignored until a migration runs
Because document databases are read-only
Because documents cannot contain nested fields
Because the schema is flexible, so new fields need no costly table migrations or rigid schema alterations
questions.explanation: Schema flexibility lets new fields be added without table migrations or rigid schema alterations, which makes document databases attractive in fast-moving development.

questions.stem: What consistency challenge arises when a customer's details are embedded in several loan documents?
options: Ensuring that a change such as an updated credit score is applied everywhere becomes more complex than in a relational database
The customer can no longer be uniquely identified
The loan documents cannot be retrieved in a single read
The credit score must be stored as a string
The documents must be normalised to 3NF first
questions.explanation: Because related data may be duplicated across documents, enforcing global consistency rules such as updating a credit score everywhere is harder than in a relational database.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of document databases?
options: Schema flexibility and developer friendliness
Strong global consistency guarantees comparable to relational systems
Natural handling of semi-structured and nested data
Close alignment with modern web and mobile architectures
Support for agile development cycles
questions.explanation: Consistency guarantees in document databases are typically weaker than in traditional relational systems; the strengths are flexibility, nested data handling, API alignment and agility.

questions.stem: In the comparison of relational and document models for loan approval, what is the relational model best for?
options: Agility and speed of development
Serving data directly to apps and APIs
Consistency, integration and complex queries
Eliminating all joins
Storing nested arrays
questions.explanation: The relational model is best for consistency, integration and complex queries, while the document model is best for agility, speed and serving data to applications.

questions.stem: How does the relational loan approval model assemble a full loan record, compared with the document model?
options: Both retrieve the record in a single read
The relational model embeds all data in one row
The document model requires joins across collections
The relational model requires multiple joins across Customer, Officer, Branch and Repayment tables, whereas the document model retrieves everything in a single read
Neither model can produce a full loan record
questions.explanation: In the relational model the loan is stored in a fact table linked to Customer, Officer, Branch and Repayment tables and needs multiple joins; the document model stores it all in one document.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between Object-Oriented Data Modelling and document data modelling?
options: Document databases cannot represent nested objects
Object-oriented models use flat tables while documents are nested
Object-oriented modelling is newer than document modelling
Document databases store methods alongside data
Object-oriented modelling bundled logic with data inside the database, whereas document databases keep only the data representation and leave logic in application code
questions.explanation: Both represent entities as rich nested objects, but OODM tried to make the database itself object-oriented with data and methods together, while document databases separate storage from application logic.
